steps.title: Create a JavaScript file with a main function
steps.instruction: Create a function named main() that will serve as the entry point for all the Map, Set, WeakMap & Symbols examples in this lesson.
steps.hint: Define a function using either 'function main() {}' or 'const main = () => {}'. The function body can be empty for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: A main function is defined and ready to contain the lesson's code examples.
successCriteria: The code contains a function named main with a valid function body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main function that will hold all our Map, Set, WeakMap & Symbols examples.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've defined a function named main with proper syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a function called main() using standard JavaScript function syntax.

steps.title: Initialize a Map with key-value pairs
steps.instruction: Inside the main() function, create a Map object with some initial key-value pairs using the Map constructor.
steps.hint: You can create a Map by calling new Map() and passing an array of [key, value] pairs as the argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main() function will contain a Map object initialized with some key-value pairs.
successCriteria: A Map object is created inside main() with at least two key-value pairs.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a Map with initial key-value pairs.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a Map, but it needs at least two key-value pairs to demonstrate the concept.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Map wasn't created correctly. Remember to use new Map() with an array of [key, value] pairs.

steps.title: Add and retrieve values from the Map
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, add new entries to the Map using the set() method, then retrieve one of those values using get() and check for existence using has().
steps.hint: First, create a Map instance. Then use map.set(key, value) to add entries, map.get(key) to retrieve a value, and map.has(key) to check if a key exists.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your main function will now create a Map, add key-value pairs, retrieve a value, and check for key existence.
successCriteria: The main function contains a Map instance with set(), get(), and has() methods called appropriately.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully used Map's set(), get(), and has() methods to manage key-value pairs.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using all three methods: set() to add entries, get() to retrieve a value, and has() to check existence.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review Map methods. You need to create a Map, add entries with set(), retrieve a value with get(), and check for a key with has().

steps.title: Iterate through Map entries
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, add a for...of loop to iterate through the Map's entries and log each key-value pair to the console.
steps.hint: Use the Map's entries() method or iterate directly over the Map object with for...of, which yields [key, value] pairs.
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will include a for...of loop that iterates over the Map's entries and logs each key-value pair.
successCriteria: A for...of loop is added inside main() that iterates through the Map's entries and logs each key-value pair.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added iteration through the Map's entries using a for...of loop.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your for...of loop correctly iterates over the Map's entries and logs each key-value pair.
steps.feedbackWrong: The iteration is missing or incorrect. Remember to use a for...of loop with the Map's entries or the Map itself.

steps.title: Initialize a Set with unique values
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create a Set object named 'uniqueNumbers' with the initial values 1, 2, 3, and 2 (notice the duplicate).
steps.hint: Use the Set constructor: new Set([values])
steps.analogousExample:
// Creating a Set with initial values
const fruitSet = new Set(['apple', 'banana', 'apple']);
steps.expectedOutcome: A Set named uniqueNumbers is created with the values 1, 2, and 3 (the duplicate 2 is automatically removed).
successCriteria: The main function contains a Set named uniqueNumbers initialized with the values 1, 2, 3, and 2.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a Set. Notice how the duplicate value 2 was automatically removed - that's one of Set's key features!
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're creating a Set named 'uniqueNumbers' with exactly the values 1, 2, 3, and 2 (including the duplicate).
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to create a Set object inside the main function. Remember to use the Set constructor with an array of initial values.

steps.title: Add, delete, and check values in the Set
steps.instruction: Inside the main function, after creating the Set, add new values to it using the add() method, delete a value using delete(), check for existence with has(), and clear all values with clear().
steps.hint: Call add() multiple times with different values, then use delete() with one of those values, check with has(), and finally call clear().
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function will include Set operations: adding values, deleting one, checking for existence, and clearing the Set.
successCriteria: The main function contains calls to add(), delete(), has(), and clear() on the Set.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the core Set operations.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some Set operations, but make sure to include all four: add, delete, has, and clear.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Set operations are missing or incorrect. Review the methods: add(), delete(), has(), and clear().

steps.title: Iterate through Set values
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, add a for...of loop to iterate through the Set's values and log each value to the console.
steps.hint: Use the syntax 'for (const value of set) { console.log(value); }' where 'set' is your Set variable name.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll be able to see each unique value from your Set printed in the console when the function runs.
successCriteria: The main function contains a for...of loop that iterates through the Set and logs each value using console.log().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added iteration through the Set values using a for...of loop.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using a for...of loop specifically for the Set and logging each value with console.log().
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to add a for...of loop inside main() that goes through your Set and logs each value.

steps.title: Create Symbols for unique identifiers
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create two Symbol values: one using Symbol() and another using Symbol('description').
steps.hint: Use the Symbol() constructor to create unique identifiers. You can optionally pass a description string.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have two Symbol variables defined inside your main function.
successCriteria: Two Symbol values are created: one without a description and one with a description string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created Symbol values. Symbols are unique primitives useful for property keys and identifiers.
steps.feedbackPartial: You created at least one Symbol, but make sure to create both: one with Symbol() and another with Symbol('description').
steps.feedbackWrong: Symbols were not created correctly. Use the Symbol() constructor to create unique identifiers.

steps.title: Use Symbols as object property keys
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create an object and use the Symbols you created earlier as property keys, then assign values to those properties.
steps.hint: You can create an object with Symbol keys using bracket notation: obj[symbol] = value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an object with properties whose keys are Symbols, demonstrating how Symbols can be used as unique identifiers for object properties.
successCriteria: An object is created inside the main function, and at least one Symbol is used as a property key with an assigned value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully used Symbols as unique property keys in an object.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the Symbols you created earlier as property keys and assigning values to them.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating an object and using bracket notation with your Symbol variables to set property values.

steps.title: Initialize a WeakMap with object keys
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create a WeakMap object using the WeakMap constructor. Initialize it with object keys (not primitive values).
steps.hint: Use the 'new WeakMap()' syntax to create a WeakMap. Remember that WeakMap keys must be objects.
steps.expectedOutcome: A WeakMap object is created inside the main function using the WeakMap constructor.
successCriteria: The main function contains a WeakMap declaration using 'new WeakMap()'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a WeakMap. WeakMaps are useful for storing private data associated with objects without preventing garbage collection.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the WeakMap constructor with 'new WeakMap()' inside the main function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The WeakMap wasn't created correctly. Remember to use 'new WeakMap()' to initialize a WeakMap object inside your main function.

steps.title: Work with WeakMap methods
steps.instruction: Inside the main function, add entries to the WeakMap using set(), retrieve values using get(), and check for existence using has().
steps.hint: Use the WeakMap you created earlier. Call set() with object keys and values, get() to retrieve values, and has() to check if a key exists.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function now includes code that demonstrates using WeakMap methods: set(), get(), and has().
successCriteria: The code includes calls to set(), get(), and has() on the WeakMap with appropriate object keys and values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added WeakMap method calls to demonstrate setting, retrieving, and checking entries.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some WeakMap method calls, but make sure to include set(), get(), and has() with appropriate object keys and values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The code doesn't yet include the required WeakMap method calls. Add set(), get(), and has() operations inside the main function.

steps.title: Call the main function and log results
steps.instruction: Call the main() function and add console.log() statements inside it to display the results of working with Map, Set, WeakMap, and Symbols.
steps.hint: Add 'main();' at the end of your file to execute the function. Inside the main() function, use console.log() to output values from your Map, Set, WeakMap, and Symbol operations.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main() function will be called, executing all the Map, Set, WeakMap, and Symbol operations, with results logged to the console.
successCriteria: The main() function is called, and console.log() statements are added inside it to display results from Map, Set, WeakMap, and Symbol operations.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully called the main() function and added console.log() statements to display the results. This completes the lesson on Map, Set, WeakMap, and Symbols.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you call main() and add console.log() statements inside it to output values from your Map, Set, WeakMap, and Symbol operations.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main() function isn't called or lacks console.log() statements. Add 'main();' at the end of the file and use console.log() inside main() to display results.
